Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Mai had been 49 when the typhoon came through her coastal town and tore apart the small apartment building where she and her husband had lived for years. She remembered the sound first, even now, not as a clear sequence but as broken pieces: the howl of the wind against the windows, a sudden crashing bang from somewhere above, the sensation of water pushing under the door, and then, in the middle of it, her own body moving without her fully understanding what was happening. One moment she had been in the kitchen trying to secure the dishes, the next she was in the dark hallway with her husband shouting for her to get low, and then the memory would skip again, leaving her with fragments that did not fit together. When she tried to tell what happened, she found herself stopping because the feeling of it rose too quickly, flooding her with the same helpless dread she had felt that night.

In the weeks afterward, Mai found that the event did not stay in the past where she wanted it. It forced its way into her mind when she least expected it, sometimes when she was standing at the fry station at the fast-food restaurant where she has worked for the past several years. The sharp hiss of oil, a tray clattering onto metal, or a delivery truck backing up with a sudden bang could make her body tense before she had time to think. She described becoming immediately on high alert when she heard unexpected or loud sounds, her attention snapping toward the noise as if she needed to locate danger before it reached her. At work, this meant she was often distracted for a few moments after a loud crash in the kitchen or a customer dropping something in the dining area, and she would have to steady herself before she could continue. She did not describe leaving work altogether, but she had come to dread the possibility of something startling happening during a busy shift.

Nighttime remained hardest. During the day, the restaurant was noisy and full of movement, which kept her focused on the tasks in front of her, but at night she found it much harder to feel safe. She said she lay awake listening for sounds from outside the apartment—wind, rain, the rattle of something loose in the building—and trouble falling asleep had become part of her routine. Even when she did drift off, she woke easily and stayed alert in the dark, her mind returning again and again to the sense that the next loud noise could mean another disaster. Her husband sometimes noticed her sitting up in bed long after he had fallen asleep, staring toward the window as if waiting for something to happen. She was not comforted by reminders that the storm had passed; what frightened her was the certainty that bad things could come without warning and there was little she could do to stop them.

As the months went on, Mai’s sense of herself changed in ways that felt almost as distressing as the memory itself. She had come to believe that she would never be able to feel normal emotions again. She described feeling flattened at times, as though the part of her that used to respond naturally to joy, sadness, or relief had been altered permanently by what she had lived through. She also said she no longer belonged anywhere. The apartment she returned to after the typhoon no longer felt fully like home, and the temporary shelter where they stayed for several weeks had felt foreign and exposing. Even now, she spoke of moving through her days as if she were unsettled in her own life, no longer fully at ease in familiar places. At work, she was able to do what was required, but the sense of being out of place followed her into breaks in the back room and into the drive home, where she would sit in the car for a few minutes before going inside.

Mai sought help after a stretch of especially poor sleep left her exhausted and increasingly distressed by the way the memory kept intruding. She said she was tired of bracing for loud sounds, tired of lying awake listening into the dark, and tired of feeling as though she had been left with a life that no longer fit. What brought her in was not only the fear that another storm could happen, but the larger fear that she would remain stuck in this state, always waiting, always on guard, and always convinced that she could not stop bad things from happening to her. She came hoping for some way to feel safe enough at night to rest, and to find out whether there was any way to recover the version of herself she believed she had lost.
